title: Welcome!
summary: A framework for benchmarking and comparing Tabular Data Synthesis tools.

content.text: The TDS Benchmark is a reproducible framework for evaluating Tabular Data Synthesis (TDS) tools across datasets, metrics, and computational settings.
It helps researchers and practitioners compare synthetic data tools for privacy, utility, robustness, distribution similarity, dependency preservation, and runtime performance.

content.caption: The benchmark connects real datasets, synthesis tools, evaluation metrics, and decision support.

content.text: Key Features
🧪 Benchmark multiple TDS tools. Run and compare tools from different model families, including GANs, VAEs, Diffusion Models, Transformers, Bayesian Networks, and Hybrid approaches.
📊 Evaluate synthetic data quality. Measure how well synthetic datasets preserve marginal distributions, dependency structures, privacy, utility, robustness, and computational performance.
⚙️ Automatic pipeline. The framework handles preprocessing, environment setup, synthetic data generation, evaluation, and result aggregation.
💻 Track computational resources. Monitor runtime, CPU usage, GPU usage, and memory consumption to understand whether a tool fits your hardware constraints.
🧭 Support tool selection. Use benchmark results together with dataset, purpose, and hardware requirements to identify suitable TDS tools for your use case.

title: Getting Started
summary: How to set up and run your first TDS benchmark experiment.

content.text: The TDS Benchmark framework evaluates and compares tabular data synthesis tools across multiple datasets, evaluation metrics, and computational performance dimensions.
Each synthesis tool requires its own folder containing the model implementation, execution script, environment configuration, and dependency files.
Repository Setup
Required Tool Structure
Each TDS tool should be placed inside its own folder named toolname-main and contain the following files.

items: Model implementation code (commonly added as a git submodule).
run_tool.py for training and synthetic data generation.
special-torch.txt for tools requiring a custom Torch installation (optional).

content.text: Dataset Preparation
Place the original dataset inside the data folder using CSV format. When benchmarking multiple tools, preprocessing and scaling the dataset beforehand is recommended to ensure fair comparison.
Run the Benchmark
Start the benchmark pipeline from the repository root. The framework will prompt you to provide an experiment configuration JSON file.
Example experiment configuration files are available in the experiments folder.
Performance Monitoring
During execution, the benchmark automatically runs the monitor_usage shell script to record CPU, GPU, memory usage, and runtime performance into CSV files. For macOS systems, use monitor_usageMac.sh.
Generated Results
After execution, the benchmark stores the generated synthetic datasets and evaluation outputs in their corresponding folders.

items: Evaluation metric outputs for synthetic data quality and utility.
Plots and aggregated benchmark visualizations inside the results folder.

content.text: For the complete list of evaluation metrics and benchmarking methodology, refer to the original benchmark paper.

title: Benchmark Pipeline
summary: Overview of the automated TDS benchmarking workflow and execution pipeline.

content.text: The benchmark pipeline implements the methodology used to evaluate TDS tools across multiple datasets, metrics, and computational performance dimensions.
The framework automates experiment configuration, dataset preprocessing, environment setup, synthetic data generation, evaluation, and statistical validation.
Pipeline Overview
The benchmark pipeline consists of six main stages: experiment configuration, preprocessing, environment setup, synthetic data generation, evaluation, and statistical validation.

content.title: Benchmark Pipeline Pseudocode
content.code:
def benchmark_pipeline(config_file, dataset_path):

    # 1. Configure experiment with JSON file
    config = read_experiment_config(config_file)

    tool = config["toolname"]
    dataset_name = config["dataset"]
    task_type = config["problem_type"]
    target_column = config["target"]
    categorical_columns = config["columns"]["categorical"]
    continuous_columns = config["columns"]["continuous"]

    # Read real dataset
    real_dataset = load_dataset(dataset_path)

    # 2. Preprocess the real dataset
    preprocessed_data = preprocess_data(
        real_dataset,
        encoding="OneHot",
        normalization="tool_specific",
        missing_value_removal=True,
        shuffling=True,
        splitting="80/20"
    )

    # 3. Configure environment
    tool_path = f"tools/{tool}-main"
    create_and_activate_conda_env(tool, tool_path)

    # Monitoring started
    monitor_process = start_monitoring()

    # 4. Tabular data synthesis: training and generation
    run_tool(
        tool_path,
        dataset_name,
        output_path=f"fake_datasets/{tool}",
        experiment_file=config_file
    )

    # Repeats synthesis 5 times

    # Monitoring stopped
    stop_monitoring(monitor_process)

    # Save performance measurements
    save_cpu_memory_metrics(tool, dataset_name)
    save_gpu_metrics(tool, dataset_name)

    # 5. Evaluate synthetic data and performance
    evaluate_results(
        marginal_distribution,
        dependency_structure,
        robustness,
        privacy,
        utility,
        performance
    )

    # 6. Statistical validation
    validate_results(
        variance,
        bootstrap,
        friedman
    )

content.text: Pipeline Components

items: Dataset preprocessing including encoding, normalization, shuffling, and train/test splitting.
Automatic Conda environment setup per TDS tool.
Synthetic data generation using standardized run_tool.py interfaces.
Resource monitoring for CPU, GPU, memory usage, and runtime.
Evaluation of marginal distributions, dependency structures, privacy, robustness, utility, and computational performance.
Statistical validation using variance analysis, bootstrap confidence intervals, and Friedman tests.

content.text: The benchmark repeats synthetic data generation multiple times per experiment to measure variance and uncertainty across the generated datasets.

title: Experiment Configuration
summary: Define the benchmark setup using JSON configuration files.

content.text: The input of the benchmark pipeline consists of two components: the experiment configuration file and the real dataset.
The configuration file is defined as a JSON dictionary containing the selected TDS tool, dataset name, machine learning problem type, target column, and dataset column types.
Configuration Parameters

items: toolname: selected TDS tool to benchmark.
dataset: dataset name used for the experiment.
target: target column used for ML utility evaluation.
mixed: columns containing mixed distributions or special values.

content.text: Example Configuration
Experiment configuration files are typically stored inside the experiments folder and passed to benchmark.py during execution.

title: Data Pre-Processing
summary: Dataset preprocessing and normalization procedures used in the benchmark.

content.text: In the second component of the benchmark pipeline, the real dataset is preprocessed before synthetic data generation and evaluation.

Most preprocessing steps are applied consistently across all TDS tools to ensure fair comparison. The main exception is normalization, where the original preprocessing strategy described by each tool is preserved.
Preprocessing Steps

items: Categorical columns are converted into numerical representations using One-Hot encoding.
Continuous columns are normalized to reduce scale differences between datasets.
Incomplete rows containing missing values are removed for the main benchmark experiments.
Additional robustness experiments are conducted using datasets with 5%, 10%, and 20% missing values.
Datasets are randomly shuffled to remove ordering bias.
Datasets are split into training and testing sets using an 80/20 ratio.

content.text: Normalization Strategies
To ensure reproducibility, the benchmark replicates the normalization strategy originally used by each TDS tool.

content.title: Tool-Specific Normalization Strategies
content.code:
PrivBayes     -> Only discrete columns, no normalization
CTGAN / TVAE  -> Mode-specific normalization applied to all X
GANBLR++      -> Ordinal encoding for all columns; numerical treated as discrete
TabDDPM       -> Normalization of complete X
GOGGLE        -> No normalization (raw tensors)
GReaT         -> No normalization; textual encoding of all columns
REaLTabFormer -> Numerical columns transformed into digit-aligned string tokens
TabuLa        -> Continuous values represented directly as text tokens
AutoDiff      -> Numerical normalization depending on implementation
TabSyn        -> Z-score normalization of all numerical columns

content.text: Post-Processing
Before evaluation, synthetic datasets are post-processed to ensure comparability with the original datasets.

items: Numerical columns are rescaled to the [0,1] range using min-max normalization.
Categorical columns are decoded back into their original representation.
Processed synthetic datasets are then used for evaluation metrics and downstream ML utility analysis.

content.text: The benchmark intentionally reproduces the preprocessing choices used in the original implementations of each TDS tool to maintain experimental consistency.

title: Environment Configuration
summary: Creation of isolated Conda environments and computational performance monitoring.

content.text: Before the synthesis process begins, the benchmark configures a dedicated execution environment for each TDS tool.
Each tool is executed inside its own Conda environment using the dependencies specified in its requirements.txt file. This ensures reproducibility and avoids dependency conflicts between tools.
Environment Setup
The benchmark automatically creates and activates a Conda environment for each synthesis tool before execution.

content.title: Environment Configuration Pseudocode
content.code:
def create_and_activate_conda_env(tool_name, tool_path):

    # 1. Start environment setup
    print("Starting environment setup")

    env_name = tool_name

    # 2. Read Python version configuration
    if python_version.txt exists in tool_path:
        python_version = read python_version.txt
    else:
        python_version = "3.9"

    # 3. Check whether Conda environment already exists
    env_list = get list of Conda environments

    if env_name exists in env_list:
        print("Environment already exists")
    else:
        print("Creating Conda environment")

        create Conda environment with:
            name = env_name
            python = python_version

        if creation fails:
            raise exception
        else:
            print("Environment created successfully")

    # 4. Configure environment variables
    conda_base = get Conda base directory

    env_path = conda_base/envs/env_name

    set PATH to include env_path/bin
    set CONDA_PREFIX = env_path
    set PYTHONUNBUFFERED = 1

    # 5. Install required packages
    requirements_path = tool_path/requirements.txt

    if requirements.txt exists:
        activate environment
        install packages using pip install -r requirements.txt

        if installation fails:
            raise exception
        else:
            print("Requirements installed successfully")
    else:
        print("No requirements.txt found")

    # 6. Finish setup
    print("Conda environment setup completed")

title: Computational Performance
summary: Hardware setup and monitoring methodology used for performance evaluation.

content.text: All benchmark experiments were executed on prosumer-grade consumer hardware to evaluate how TDS tools perform outside specialized high-performance computing environments.

The benchmark system consisted of 32GB RAM, an Intel Core i9-12900H processor (14 cores, 20 threads), and an external NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 24GB VRAM connected through a Razer Core X eGPU enclosure.
Experiments were conducted on Linux to minimize background processes and provide consistent performance measurements.
Reference Hardware

items: Intel Core i9-12900H (12th Gen, 14 cores, 20 threads)
Razer Core X eGPU enclosure with 1000W PSU

content.text: Performance Monitoring
A lightweight monitoring script was executed in parallel with each benchmark experiment to record computational resource usage throughout training and synthetic data generation.
The monitoring process starts immediately before the synthesis process and terminates after completion, ensuring full coverage of the workload.

items: System memory usage measured using free.
1 Hz sampling frequency with timestamped CSV logging.

content.text: Monitoring Script

content.title: Computational Performance Monitoring Script
content.code:
#!/bin/bash

# This script monitors CPU, system memory, and GPU usage

cpu_mem_output_file="cpu_mem_usage.csv"
gpu_output_file="gpu_usage.csv"

# Check if nvidia-smi is available for GPU monitoring
if ! command -v nvidia-smi &> /dev/null
then
    echo "nvidia-smi could not be found, GPU monitoring will not be available."
    gpu_monitoring=0
else
    gpu_monitoring=1
fi

# Initialize CPU and memory CSV file
echo "Timestamp,CPU Usage (%),Memory Usage (%)" > "$cpu_mem_output_file"

# Initialize GPU CSV file
echo "Timestamp,GPU Number,GPU Usage (%),GPU Memory Used (MB),GPU Memory Total (MB)" \
  > "$gpu_output_file"

# Function to get CPU and memory usage
get_cpu_mem_usage() {
    cpu=$(mpstat 1 1 | awk '/Average:/ {print 100 - $12}' | tr -d '\n')
    mem=$(free | grep Mem | awk '{printf "%.2f", $3/$2 * 100.0}' | tr -d '\n')
    echo "$cpu,$mem"
}

# Function to get GPU usage
get_gpu_usage() {
    if [ "$gpu_monitoring" -eq 1 ]; then
        nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,memory.used,memory.total \
                   --format=csv,noheader,nounits
    else
        echo "N/A,N/A,N/A,N/A"
    fi
}

# Collect monitoring data every second
while true
do
    timestamp=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

    cpu_mem_usage=$(get_cpu_mem_usage)
    echo "$timestamp,$cpu_mem_usage" >> "$cpu_mem_output_file"

    gpu_usage=$(get_gpu_usage)
    while IFS= read -r line
    do
        echo "$timestamp,$line" >> "$gpu_output_file"
    done <<< "$gpu_usage"

    sleep 1
done

content.text: Experimental Control Strategies
To reduce noise and improve measurement consistency, several experimental control strategies were applied during benchmarking.
Limitations
The monitoring setup was intentionally designed to remain lightweight and minimally intrusive. As a result, measurements are collected at the system level rather than per process.
Metrics such as disk I/O and memory swapping are not explicitly tracked because including all possible system-level measurements would increase monitoring overhead and complexity.
The benchmark prioritizes reproducibility and low-overhead monitoring to avoid influencing the observed computational performance of the TDS tools.

title: Tabular Data Synthesis
summary: Training and synthetic data generation workflow used across all TDS tools.

content.text: The synthesis process is the central component of the benchmark pipeline. Each TDS tool is executed through a standardized wrapper script called run_tool.py.
This script connects the benchmark framework with the original implementation of each synthesis tool while preserving a consistent execution pipeline across experiments.
Synthesis Workflow
The benchmark performs hardware checks, initializes the synthesis model, trains the model, generates synthetic samples, post-processes the outputs, and stores the resulting synthetic datasets.

content.title: run_tool.py Pseudocode
content.code:
def run_tool(tool, prepared_data, output_path):

    # 1. Hardware check
    if gpu_is_available():
        set_cuda_device()
    else:
        set_cpu_mode()

    set_required_environment_variables()

    # 2. Repeat full training + synthesis 5 times
    for repetition in range(1, 6):

        # Use predefined seed for this repetition
        set_random_seed(predefined_seeds[repetition])

        # Train model
        model = initialize_model(tool)
        train_model(model, prepared_data)

        # Generate synthetic data
        synthetic_data = sample(model, size=len(prepared_data))

        synthetic_table = postprocess(synthetic_data)

        # Save result
        save_csv(
            synthetic_table,
            f"{output_path}/{tool}_{repetition}.csv"
        )

    return

content.text: Benchmark Logic
All TDS tools follow the same benchmark structure, even though their internal architectures and training procedures differ.

items: GPU or CPU configuration depending on available hardware.
Fixed predefined random seeds shared across all tools.
Training and synthetic data generation repeated five times.
Post-processing and storage of generated synthetic datasets.
Standardized output format across all benchmark experiments.

content.text: Reproducibility
Using the same seeds across all tools ensures fair comparison under identical randomness conditions.
The tool-specific implementation details are isolated inside each run_tool.py file, allowing the benchmark framework to evaluate diverse TDS tools using a unified and reproducible pipeline.
Each benchmark experiment produces five synthetic datasets per tool-dataset pair to measure variance and improve robustness of the evaluation results.

title: Evaluation
summary: Evaluation metrics and procedures used to assess synthetic data quality, utility, privacy, and computational performance.

content.text: The evaluation component computes the benchmark metrics for each synthetic dataset generated during the synthesis process together with the recorded computational performance logs.
The benchmark evaluates synthetic datasets across marginal distributions, dependency structures, robustness, privacy preservation, machine learning utility, and computational performance.
Evaluation Workflow

content.title: evaluate_results.py Pseudocode

content.text: Evaluation Dimensions

items: Privacy preservation using nearest-neighbor distance metrics.

content.text: Column-Based Metrics
Most evaluation metrics are computed directly between corresponding real and synthetic columns following their standard mathematical definitions.
Continuous columns are evaluated using Wasserstein Distance and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics, while categorical columns are evaluated using Jensen-Shannon and Kullback-Leibler divergence.
Dependency Structure
To quantify relationship preservation, the benchmark computes fixed column-pair correlations for both real and synthetic datasets.
Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, and Point-Biserial correlations are compared by measuring the absolute difference between real and synthetic correlation values.
A difference of zero indicates perfect preservation of the original dependency structure for a given column pair.
Privacy Metrics
Privacy evaluation uses Distance to Closest Record (DCR) and Nearest Neighbor Distance Ratio (NNDR) to determine whether synthetic samples are excessively similar to real records.
Before privacy evaluation, synthetic datasets are post-processed so that real and synthetic data share the same feature representation.
Machine Learning Utility
The benchmark evaluates downstream ML utility by training multiple machine learning models on synthetic data and testing them on the real test dataset.
This measures whether the synthetic datasets preserve the predictive information contained in the original data.
Classification Models
Regression Models
The benchmark computes evaluation metrics for all five synthetic datasets generated per experiment and aggregates the results to improve robustness and statistical reliability.

title: Validation
summary: Statistical significance, variance, and uncertainty estimation used in the benchmark.

content.text: The final component of the benchmark pipeline validates the evaluation results using statistical significance testing, variance estimation, and uncertainty analysis.
Because many machine learning models contain stochastic training processes, repeated executions of the same experiment can produce different outcomes even under identical settings.
To ensure robust and interpretable benchmark results, the framework evaluates variability across repeated runs and measures whether observed differences between tools are statistically meaningful.
Validation Workflow

items: Five repetitions are executed per tool–dataset pair using different predefined random seeds.
Mean and standard deviation are computed across repetitions.
Bootstrap resampling is used to estimate confidence intervals.
A Friedman test is applied to evaluate statistical significance between tools.

content.text: Variance and Uncertainty
Variance measures how stable the benchmark results remain across repeated executions, while uncertainty estimates the expected range of the true performance.
The benchmark uses standard deviation to quantify variability and bootstrap confidence intervals to estimate uncertainty.
Bootstrap resampling is particularly suitable because only five repetitions are available per experiment, making parametric assumptions unreliable.
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
For each metric and tool–dataset pair, the five benchmark results are repeatedly resampled to generate a distribution of mean values.
Statistical Significance
The benchmark uses the Friedman test to determine whether observed differences between TDS tools are statistically significant or caused by randomness.
The Friedman test ranks tools independently on each dataset and compares their average ranks across all datasets.
Experimental Design
The benchmark incorporates several design choices to improve result stability and reduce random effects.

items: Consistent preprocessing and evaluation pipeline across all tools.
Repeated runs with controlled random seeds.

content.text: Computational Considerations

Running repeated experiments for all tools and datasets is computationally expensive. The benchmark therefore balances statistical robustness with practical feasibility by using five repetitions per experiment.
The complete benchmark required thousands of synthesis runs and several months of computation on the described hardware setup.
The benchmark combines repeated runs, bootstrap confidence intervals, and Friedman significance testing to ensure that the reported differences between TDS tools are robust and interpretable.
